summary: Traverse or transform a binary (or n-ary) tree using recursive DFS (pre/in/post-order) or iterative BFS (level order) to compute properties, search, or rebuild structure.
lesson: Trees are graphs with a fixed hierarchy (a single root, no cycles), which means most tree problems decompose naturally: the answer for a node is defined in terms of the answers for its children. That's why recursive DFS (compute left, compute right, combine) is the default tool -- height, sum, balance, and lowest-common-ancestor problems all follow this same "solve the subtree, combine with the current node" shape. BFS (level order, via a queue) is what you reach for instead whenever the question is actually about levels or "shortest path" in an unweighted tree, since DFS doesn't naturally expose that structure.
recognize_when: Input is explicitly a binary tree / BST / n-ary tree with node.left, node.right (or children)
You need a property defined recursively on subtrees (height, sum, balance, LCA)
The problem asks for level-by-level output or the shortest path in an unweighted tree (favors BFS)
You need to validate or construct a tree from a traversal order
Path-sum or root-to-leaf style problems that naturally decompose into subproblems

complexity.notes: Every node is visited once; DFS space is the recursion stack depth (O(h), worst case O(n) for a skewed tree, O(log n) if balanced). BFS space is O(w), the max width of a level, due to the queue.

gotchas: Missing the base case (node is None) causes infinite recursion or AttributeError
Reaching for recursive DFS when the problem actually wants level-order output or shortest unweighted path -- use BFS with a queue (collections.deque) instead
Confusing traversal orders (pre/in/post) when reconstructing a tree or when order of visiting matters for the answer
examples: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
